A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ToMAP study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, tables and equations can be matched across the reorganization. Visual inspection resolves the chart-label extraction issues.

before.justification: v1 reports original persuasion benchmarks, ablations, training analyses and evaluations of the counterclaim and attitude predictors.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds SFT comparisons, human assessment of LLM attitudes and additional dialogue cases.

M1.justification: The counterclaim predictor, BGE-M3 plus MLP attitude predictor, ToM-augmented inputs, PPO training and reward functions remain unchanged. Auxiliary rewards move to Appendix C, and the new pseudocode documents the existing procedure.

E1.justification: Coverage remains CMV, Anthropic and args.me, with Qwen-7B, LLaMa-8B and Phi-4 persuadees. The human validation rates attitudes in the retained LLM-dialogue setting; it does not introduce human persuadees or a new persuasion domain. Added SFT data and dialogue cases stay within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds SFT to the main comparison. Its Table 2 adds Gemma-3, LLaMa3.1, Deepseek-R1 and GPT-4o to the with/without-ToM comparison, whose counterpart in v1 Figure 3 included only Base and ToMAP. Conversely, ToMAP-rand and ToMAP-max disappear from the attitude-predictor ablation.

E3.justification: The main three-round evaluation and PPO configuration remain unchanged. v2 adds a human-rating protocol using 50 conversations, ten per attitude level, and an SFT configuration using 5k conversations for one epoch. The with/without-ToM comparison now reports Qwen-only averages rather than dataset-specific Qwen and LLaMa results. v2 also describes the ground-truth variant as trained with its attitude information, whereas v1 explicitly shares ToMAP parameters; this establishes a reported setting change, not a verified rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 5.1 tests whether human judgments agree with persuadee self-reports, addressing the validity of the evaluation signal. Appendix E adds contrasting minimum-wage dialogues across three persuadees. The ToM-use ablation expands to larger persuaders, while the random-attitude and maximum-agreement robustness controls are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three trials. v2 removes v1's standard-deviation bound of 0.97 and its one-tailed t-test reporting p < 0.01 for RL versus ToMAP. It adds Cohen's kappa for human–LLM agreement, without reporting uncertainty around that estimate.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes all nine RL scores, with the reported average moving from 13.84 to 14.60. ToMAP changes from 8.82 to 10.77 on CMV/LLaMa and from 24.19 to 22.25 on args.me/Phi-4, retaining its 17.48 average. v2 adds SFT results averaging 12.49 and human agreement results of 0.76 accuracy and 0.70 kappa. Ablation entries also change, including the ground-truth args.me score from 16.65 to 17.65 under its revised setting description.

T1.justification: The dialogue definitions, balanced agreement score, reward equations, optimization objective and predictor formulation are mathematically unchanged. Prompt notation is clarified, and existing equations or identities are relocated. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstracts retain the same contributions and headline claims: two ToM modules with RL, a 3B persuader, 39.4% relative advantage over GPT-4o, reduced repetition and effective long conversations. Condensed introduction and conclusion passages do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations supporting self-reported attitudes through human agreement, attributing SFT's weaker results to its static approach, and explaining persuadee differences through learned conversational styles. It removes v1's substantive limitations concerning reward gaming and fabricated evidence, training against one persuadee, and testing only 3B persuaders. Discussion of inaccurate attitude information is also removed with the noise ablations.

D1.justification: v2 adds conversation-pipeline pseudocode and SFT details: selection by positive agreement shift, 5k conversations, one epoch and learning rate 1e-5. A new reproducibility statement reports supplementary code inclusion, which the PDFs alone cannot verify. Existing PPO/MLP settings and hardware disclosures remain, but Figure 4 no longer specifies EMA smoothing with alpha 0.3.

R1.justification: v2 adds Carrasco-Farre (2024) on cognitive effort and persuasion, while removing Cialdini (2001), Hackenburg et al. (2025), ToMBench and Amirizaniani et al. (2024). The central positioning at the intersection of persuasion, RL and theory of mind remains. The anonymous concurrent RL work is retained despite its changed title.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, component explanations, ablation narrative and conclusion undergo substantial condensation or rewriting. Appendices are extensively reordered: prompts move from B to A, training from D to C, and ToM details from A to D. Auxiliary rewards leave the main text, and reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Table 1 is transposed and reorganized into persuadee groups with explicit out-of-domain headings. The six heatmaps in v1 Figure 3 are replaced by an aggregate ablation table, while v2 Figure 3 introduces a human–LLM confusion matrix. Training-table structure, dialogue-example panels, figure placement and document-wide typography/layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful SFT comparisons, human validation of LLM attitude reports and pipeline documentation. However, it removes explicit reward-gaming and generalization limitations together with the main uncertainty/significance disclosure. Revised RL scores also leave Section 4.2's claimed 26.14% ToMAP gain inconsistent with Table 1, whose averages imply about 19.7%. These evidential gains and losses do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.
